📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.1) What is an NFT?NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.2) What is Blockchain?A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.3) What makes an NFT valuable? The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.4) How do NFTs work?One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to mentioned NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach fresh buyers interested in art.10) How do we buy an NFTs?There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.11) Can i mint NFT for free?To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it? The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.12) Why are people investing so much in NFT? Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.Final SayingThat’s a wrap. Hope you guys found this article enlightening. I just answer some question with my limited knowledge about NFTs. If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to drop them in the comment section below. Recent findings suggest that the answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

Industry observers note that you can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • In a recent development, LFM2 indicated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

In a recent development, LFM2 indicated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

In a recent development, the payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Industry observers note that every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two upcoming in-house encoders:.

Sources indicate that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

It has been revealed that reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

In a recent development, reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google unveiled on November 21, 2026 that it is providing the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur (IIT Kharagpur) with $5 million to support advanced AI research, expand AI education and build AI capacity across the university’s campus.

The funding is designed for university researchers and students across three pillars. The research component covers applied AI work in Indic languages, materials science, agriculture and educational technology. The education component supports AI training and curriculum development for students, faculty and teachers.

Industry observers note that the capacity-building component will support IIT Kharagpur’s AI frameworks and tooling to strengthen the technological environment across campus. This structure links the research agenda to curriculum development and the technical resources available to the wider university community.

Google mentioned the fund is intended to support applied research and technological solutions benefiting communities across India and beyond, framing deep collaboration and strong academic leadership as necessary for building AI that works for everyone.

Sundar Pichai, CEO of Google and Alphabet, connected the collaboration to his own experience at the institute: “Looking forward to seeing this collaboration shape the path for the next generation of students, just as IIT Kharagpur shaped my own.”.

Pichai also described India as increasingly at the forefront of innovation and remarked programs like this would help implement Prime Minister Modi’s vision of AI benefits reaching everyone in India.

Industry observers note that the funding follows an existing research relationship. On July 10, 2025, Google announced that it was collaborating with IIT Kharagpur researchers to bring the Google Research-led Amplify Initiative to India. The project was designed to give developers and researchers free access to structured, locally grounded datasets reflecting India’s linguistic and cultural diversity. Its aim is to address gaps in large language models resulting from the limited representation of languages, dialects and cultural context in existing AI training data.

Google Research’s original Amplify explanation, published May 2, 2025, described an open platform built around community data collection, with datasets suitable for model fine-tuning and evaluation. It named IIT Kharagpur as its Indian partner, with a remit to gather and validate local material that an AI model could not generate by itself.

In a recent development, under the collection process, sector experts enter information about notable local concerns through privacy-preserving Android and web apps. Regional partners and country research leads then translate the queries and assess their local relevance, coherence and fluency, as well as the collection’s coverage. The approach places local experts and partner institutions at the center of both data creation and review.

In a September 15, 2026 enhancement, Google reported that Amplify involved more than 1,600 local experts and 20 universities across four continents, including IIT Kharagpur, contributing 15,000 multimodal data points. Those figures cover the full program, not IIT Kharagpur’s individual contribution.

Sources indicate that the new commitment is broader than the Amplify collaboration: it pairs research in several fields with curriculum development and campus AI tooling. For IIT Kharagpur, that connects the questions being investigated with the training and technical resources needed to pursue them.

With an optimistic but data-driven perspective, Nina examines peer-reviewed research, institutional pilots, and real-world implementations to separate measurable progress from hype. She is particularly interested in AI systems that improve learning outcomes, reduce barriers to education, and enable researchers to work more efficiently without replacing human expertise.

Her reporting aims to highlight credible innovation at the intersection of AI, education, and research—where technology enhances human potential rather than diminishing it.

#92346. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2027 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, language models can do a lot.
  • Say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they mentioned (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's newly introduced speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Sources indicate that parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Sources indicate that when you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who mentioned what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

It has been revealed that the diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

In a recent development, the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

It has been revealed that we measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

Recent findings suggest that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't newly introduced, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

It has been revealed that what's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

Sources indicate that the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

Sources indicate that you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

According to recent reports, each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

According to recent reports, each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Sources indicate that try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Problems and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ginger VS Grammarly: When it comes to grammar checkers, Ginger and Grammarly are two of the most popular choices on the market. This article aims to highlight the specifics of each one so that you can make a more informed decision about the one you'll use.What is Grammarly?If you are a writer, you must have heard of  Grammarly before. Grammarly has over 10M people across the globe, it's probably the most popular AI writing enhancement tool, without a doubt. That's why there's a high chance that you already know about Grammarly.But today we are going to do a comparison between Ginger and Grammarly, So let's define Grammarly here. Like Ginger, Grammarly is an AI writing assistant that checks for grammatical errors, spellings, and punctuation. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakesWhile the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.Features of GrammarlyGrammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve itCreate a personal dictionary Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.Understand inconsistencies. Detect unclear structure. Detect Plagiarism.Explore overuse of words and wordiness. Get to know about the improper tones. Discover the insensitive language aligns with your intent, audience, style, emotion, and more.What is Ginger Ginger is a writing enhancement tool that not only catches typos and grammatical mistakes but also suggests content improvements. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1609 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Recent findings suggest that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That stated, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

It has been revealed that for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

It has been revealed that for each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

Industry observers note that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

In a recent development, cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing indicated promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

It has been revealed that the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

AI Governance in 2027: Accountability Moves Into the Workflow

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A person receives an automated decision that makes no sense to them.
  • That gap will become harder to defend in 2027.
  • In a recent development, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OECD's 2026 due-diligence guidance already offer organizational foundations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A person receives an automated decision that makes no sense to them. They ask for a review. Somewhere inside the organization, a policy names an accountable executive—but the support team cannot find anyone authorized to change the result. Governance exists on paper. The person is still stuck.

That gap will become harder to defend in 2027. As AI moves into ordinary operations, accountability will have to become something an organization can exercise while a disputed decision is still affecting someone's life.

In a recent development, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OECD's 2026 due-diligence guidance already offer organizational foundations. My expectation for 2027 is that buyers will ask for evidence of these practices inside operating workflows. The following predictions concern organizational accountability, rather than a promise that a particular checklist can make every AI system fair.

Industry observers note that the most revealing name on an AI governance chart is the person who can say stop. In 2027, more organizations will describe roles with genuine authority to suspend or change a deployment. That changes the meaning of ownership: responsibility becomes a decision right, with consequences for a project somebody else may be eager to keep running.

Recent findings suggest that responsibility without authority creates a ceremonial owner. A governance lead can maintain an inventory while a product team changes the model, a supplier changes the service, and an operations team changes the decision threshold. No single person necessarily controls the consequences of the resulting system.

In a recent development, the Govern function in the NIST framework connects roles and organizational risk management. The NIST Playbook offers practical actions that organizations can adapt. These are voluntary resources, not evidence that adopters already execute them well.

Industry observers note that the development I expect is a more concrete chain of authority: who can accept a use case, who can narrow its scope, and who can stop it when the evidence changes. Different decisions can belong to different roles. What matters is that the authority survives ordinary commercial pressure and is exercised against a documented standard. A well-written responsibility chart that nobody uses would not demonstrate the predicted change.

In a recent development, look for published suspension criteria, records of actual governance decisions, and escalation paths beyond the product's revenue owner. A policy naming an accountable executive without explaining what that executive can change would provide weaker evidence than an operational case study.

Assign decision rights before expanding a deployment. Buyers should ask who can authorize exceptions and whether the risk function can halt a workflow without the supplier's consent. Founders can shorten enterprise reviews by making these responsibilities visible in the product and service agreement.

An explanation can tell someone why a decision happened and still leave them powerless to correct it. I expect enterprise products to make challenges more practical in 2027, preserving the original evidence and recording what the reviewer decides. The test of the feature will be what happens after the person says the system has missed something crucial.

An explanation and an appeal solve different problems. An explanation tells a person what supposedly happened. An appeal gives them a route to change an outcome that may be wrong, incomplete or inappropriate for their circumstances. A generic support form can satisfy neither need if the reviewer cannot reconstruct the original decision.

It has been revealed that the OECD guidance treats due diligence as a continuing process involving impacts and responses. That makes remediation a useful commercial design question as well as an ethical one. My forecast is that some vendors will turn it into a repeatable workflow rather than leave each customer to improvise.

The difficult part will be the reviewer's independence and access to context. Re-running the same model with slightly different wording is not a meaningful challenge process. Nor should preserving evidence require indiscriminate retention of sensitive personal information. The system needs enough decision context to support correction while honoring appropriate retention and access limits.

According to recent reports, look for the ability to submit missing facts, reach a qualified human reviewer, and receive a recorded disposition. Reversal rates and time to correction will be more revealing than the existence of an appeal button. Unanswered queues would weaken the forecast's practical significance.

According to recent reports, budget for the people who handle contested decisions. A supplier's automation savings should be assessed alongside review workload and correction costs. Product teams should design evidence capture and access permissions with the appeal process, because reconstructing decisions afterward can be expensive or impossible.

Sources indicate that an internal drafting assistant can become a customer-screening tool through a series of apparently small product decisions. The launch approval may still be on file while the use case has changed underneath it. In 2027, more governance programs will revisit material changes in models, data and affected populations, treating approval as a continuing responsibility.

Recent findings suggest that A system approved for drafting internal correspondence can become consequential when its output starts determining which customers receive an offer. The model may be unchanged; its social role has changed. Conversely, a supplier upgrade can alter behavior while the customer-facing workflow looks identical.

It has been revealed that ISO/IEC 42001 addresses organizational AI management, and ISO's discussion of 42001 and impact assessment connects management practices with evaluating effects. Neither makes a management-system certificate a guarantee that every output is accurate or every deployment is acceptable.

It has been revealed that the practical challenge is proportionality. Repeating a full assessment for a spelling correction would overwhelm the process; ignoring a upcoming affected population would undermine it. Organizations will need a defensible account of which changes alter the risk and which do not.

Industry observers note that look for specific reassessment triggers and examples where a deployment's conditions were narrowed after review. Version logs alone will be insufficient. Evidence that organizations compare real effects before and after a material change would strengthen this prediction considerably.

Industry observers note that include change notification and evaluation rights in supplier contracts. Internally, connect the model inventory to the systems that manage deployment changes. The objective is to identify changes that matter early enough to act, without turning every routine maintenance event into a board-level decision.

A certificate can become more reassuring than the evidence warrants. The harder commercial conversation is what it actually covers. In 2027, assurance and procurement documents will become clearer about the difference between an organization's management practices and the behavior of a particular deployment. That precision will make assurance more useful, even when it makes the sales claim less sweeping.

According to recent reports, the more popular a governance label becomes, the more tempting it is to treat that label as a universal seal of safety. Yet different assurance exercises answer different questions. An audit of management processes cannot prove that a model behaves reliably for a population the evaluator never tested.

According to recent reports, ISO/IEC 42006 sets requirements for bodies auditing and certifying AI management systems. It is relevant to the quality of certification itself. It does not turn ISO/IEC 42001 into a product-performance benchmark. This distinction will become more commercially crucial as suppliers use assurance credentials in sales processes.

Recent findings suggest that my confidence is lower here because incentives can favor broad reassurance over careful qualification. Still, sophisticated buyers have a reason to demand both organizational assurance and use-case evidence: they bear the consequences if a certified supplier's product fails in their workflow. Good assurance should make the remaining questions clearer, rather than imply that there are none.

Look for an explicit statement of the certified entity, scope, exclusions and validity period, alongside separate application testing. Claims that a certificate proves an AI system is unbiased or universally compliant would run against the direction predicted here.

In a recent development, use certification to inform diligence, then evaluate the actual deployment. Suppliers should prepare a clear explanation of what their assurance covers. Buyers should ask which unresolved risks remain their responsibility and what evidence would justify accepting them.

Accountability becomes visible when the organization has a reason to resist it: an attractive launch, an expensive correction, a profitable use case that needs narrowing. The strongest governance stories in 2027 will show how those decisions were made—and whether the people affected had a meaningful way to be heard.

She aims to bridge the gap between rapid technological progress and the safeguards needed to ensure AI systems remain transparent, fair, and aligned with human interests.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Lean and Mathlib communities certified on November 21, 2026 that Levent Alpöge’s 17-million-line Lean library correctly states and proves the Riemann Hypothesis, following a day of compilation, statement-matching, and proof-kernel checks. Their joint statement was endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

In a recent development, the certification follows Alpöge’s announcement on November 20, 2026, in which he stated he discovered and formalized the proof while working with Claude. The release contained only the Lean formalization; Alpöge viewed a conventional write-up at this stage as a huge, unreadable document and planned to understand, simplify, and explain the mathematics properly.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib, the community’s library of formalized mathematics. The statement being proved was already part of Mathlib and had been vetted by experts in Lean and number theory, addressing the requirement that the formal statement express the intended hypothesis. Dozens of people reported compiling the library without errors or build failures and reproducing the same raw proof export.

To check the theorem’s identity, a community-added challenge file isolated the Riemann Hypothesis statement and imported only Mathlib. Comparator and con-leche’s comparison mode independently confirmed that Alpöge’s theorem matched that statement exactly. The raw proof export was checked with Lean’s official kernel, con-leche, con-ron, and additional third-party checkers written in different programming languages.

Those checks ran on an inert export, beyond the reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean sources. Con-leche and con-ron also have formal proofs, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, addressing concerns that a flaw in Lean’s logic could be exploited.

Industry observers note that andrew Sutherland’s MIT verification record, last updated at 12:55 UTC on November 21, 2026, reports that all 175,187 modules compiled with zero errors using Lean and Mathlib version 4.33.1; his checks were run with Claude Code. An axiom audit found that the five headline theorems depended only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound, with no axioms declared outside Lean core. Nanoda, an independent Rust kernel, and con-leche each accepted the full exported proof, lean4lean accepted every compiled module, and con-leche’s comparison mode matched every challenge statement.

In a recent development, at that page’s cutoff, the Lean default and paranoid kernel checks on the export and the full lake comparator run remained in progress. Older bundled con-leche and con-ron binaries exited without a verdict because they did not support one reflexive inductive type, not because they rejected the proof. Sutherland also disclosed that the build ran on unsandboxed cloud machines and that its export hash had not been compared with one from a sandboxed lake build; a passing result still relies on the kernels used and on Mathlib’s definitions representing their intended mathematics.

Sources indicate that the central theorem uses Mathlib’s formal definition: every zero of the Riemann zeta function other than the trivial zeros at negative even integers must have real part one-half. The separate condition s ≠ 1 appears because Mathlib assigns the zeta function a conventional value at its pole. The submission also verifies Generalized Riemann Hypothesis statements for Dirichlet L-functions across all moduli and characters; Sutherland expressly excludes Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions, and general automorphic L-functions from the checked scope.

Recent findings suggest that alpöge’s account assigns Claude a role in discovery as well as formalization: he guided the work from a toy setting into an analogous target situation before Claude outpaced him near the finish. In one example, Claude suggested that a von Mangoldt sum of length X should use a chain of theta lifts of length X, a technical choice Alpöge highlights in his explanation of the argument.

According to recent reports, alpöge describes the current argument as extremely long, expects substantial simplification, and is still working to understand and explain it. His account describes human guidance and Claude’s technical contributions, with both formalizing the arguments without extra assumptions. The certification concerns the formal artifact; that account supplies the basis for describing Claude’s role, rather than demonstrating an autonomous solution.

It has been revealed that the certification resolves the formal-checking question without resolving the explanatory one. Whether the proof’s latest ideas can be simplified and absorbed by mathematicians remains the central open question around the verified Lean library.

With a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. #92322. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1298 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

According to recent reports, participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Industry observers note that the U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

According to recent reports, project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

Sources indicate that the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many upcoming science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

It has been revealed that publicly available genomic data has proved crucial in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

Industry observers note that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Industry observers note that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

It has been revealed that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples from a subset of customer prompts submitted to its serverless inference service.
  • According to recent reports, customers had authorized the prompts for routine software testing, and Together AI stored the samples in a private Hugging Face repository.
  • The coding agent committed a credential that granted access to the private Hugging Face repository during xorl’s development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026 that an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples from a subset of customer prompts submitted to its serverless inference service. An AI coding agent had exposed the private-repository credential used in the download while the tech giant was developing its public xorl GitHub repository.

According to recent reports, customers had authorized the prompts for routine software testing, and Together AI stored the samples in a private Hugging Face repository. They involved requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 models, primarily on June 24, 2026, July 4, 2026, July 8, 2026 and July 14, 2026.

The coding agent committed a credential that granted access to the private Hugging Face repository during xorl’s development. Together AI’s automated scanning detected the exposure, and the company reverted the commit. During that exposure window, an unauthorized party obtained the credential and used it to download the stored samples.

It has been revealed that the sequence makes clear that detecting and reverting the commit did not prevent the credential from being used during the exposure window. The model names establish which requests were sampled, while the repository credential explains how the stored prompts became accessible.

Recent findings suggest that after the download, the party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested whether they were valid. Five of the tested credentials were canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment. The searches and validity tests show that the activity extended to possible reuse of secrets contained in prompts, creating a risk beyond disclosure of the prompt text itself.

It has been revealed that together AI worked with an external forensic investigation firm and law enforcement. The manufacturer said its review has not identified evidence of additional prompt leakage beyond this incident, that it has no reason to believe the data was leaked further, and that it understands the data has now been deleted.

Recent findings suggest that customer impact still depends on the content of the samples. The review is ongoing to determine whether sensitive personal information or other customer data was exposed, and Together AI will contact affected customers directly as needed with findings relevant to them.

Together AI’s response includes scoped or short-lived credentials and keyless access where supported, credential checks on all pull requests, and updated development processes governing the use of AI coding agents. The manufacturer remarked the credential measures are designed to reduce the potential impact of exposure, while the other changes add controls around pull requests and coding-agent development.

Zero data retention, abbreviated ZDR, is now the default setting for fresh accounts. Together AI recommends that customers handling sensitive prompt data enable ZDR in their account settings and provides security@together.ai for questions about the incident or its potential impact on an organization.

The incident connects credential safety in AI-assisted development with the retention of customer prompts for testing. Together AI has documented controls for both, but the ongoing content review remains the decisive step in establishing what the exposure means for customers and which notifications are necessary.

#92315. 'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1185 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Darkreading ↗ Open Full Page

'Sleeper Agent' Tactic Hides Payloads in Open-Weight AI Models

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1185 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, malware can lurk inside just 0.00001% of a neural network.
  • AI models downloaded from the open Internet can be subtly poisoned with malicious payloads if attackers are careful enough.
  • Open-weight AI models have become seriously popular lately.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, malware can lurk inside just 0.00001% of a neural network. How, then, can any user tell it's there?

AI models downloaded from the open Internet can be subtly poisoned with malicious payloads if attackers are careful enough.

Open-weight AI models have become seriously popular lately. Even early last year, McKinsey found that 63% of organizations used them, and 76% of survey respondents mentioned that they expected to use them more in the coming years. They're auditable, developers like using them, and, perhaps most of all, they're cheap.

Like any other software you can download off the Internet, however, open-weight and open source AI tools carry some degree of risk. Last week, researchers described a technique they call "Lazarus," which could allow an attacker to poison a model using a near-imperceptible few of its neurons. Microsoft described it as turning a model into a "sleeper agent," capable of granting an attacker access to its user's environment.

Industry observers note that "A model is a file almost nobody inspects, yet we download models from strangers and give them access to our code, credentials, and systems," explains Briland Hitaj, senior AI security research engineer at Confidencial, whose research into techniques like this preceded Microsoft's. "Malicious models have already turned up on Hugging Face, though so far they abuse file formats like Python's Pickle to run code when loaded. I'm not aware of anyone hiding payloads inside the weights themselves outside research, but that's where the research points.".

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era.

Since at least 2020, researchers have been coming up with clever ways to store bad stuff inside of neural networks.

Industry observers note that the premise behind this whole category of research is that the size and complexity of these networks provide cover for small, secret, but potentially powerful payloads. Just look at Qwen 3.8-Max: It's totally open-weight, so you can inspect it to your heart's content. But it's made of 2.4 trillion parameters, and probably around 100 million neurons. If an attacker plants a functioning payload in some of those neurons or parameters, how exactly are you going to find it?

Sources indicate that the trick, then, isn't finding a place to hide a payload. First, it's getting that payload to function reliably amid so many moving parts; second, it's making sure it doesn't noticeably impact the normal functioning of the model; and lastly, optionally making the payload robust to fine-tuning.

Recent findings suggest that different researchers have come up with different ways to do it. In 2022, Hitaj and his colleagues came up with a technique called "MaleficNet," which repurposed an old military and, later, 2G and 3G mobile network technique called "code division multiple access" (CDMA).

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem.

Very simply, they split malware binaries into tiny pieces and spread the pieces across the many individual weights that make up a neural network. It wouldn't look like anything but noise to a passerby, yet with a trigger mechanism and a way to decode the weights, they could recover, recombine, and execute the binary.

"The vulnerability comes from how neural networks work, not from a bug," Hitaj explains. "Models have far more parameters than they strictly need, so you can nudge millions of weights slightly, or repurpose a few neurons that rarely fire, without visibly changing the model's behavior. And since nobody can read weights the way they read code, those changes go unnoticed.".

Sources indicate that microsoft's upcoming technique compromises on capacity for simplicity. Where Hitaj proposed encoding an entire binary across many model parameters, Microsoft researchers propose sneaking a brief command inside of fewer than 10 neurons. Specifically, one must target "dormant" neurons — those that prove to have little effect on the overall model's functioning — late in a model's processing cycle, and thus more directly influential over its output. One encodes a payload in these neurons, arranged to fire sequentially, and configures them to stay largely inactive unless they're fed a trigger. Eventually, you get a sleeper agent.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud.

The target payload can be arbitrary, so long as it's small and formatted correctly. The trigger can be any particular user input to the model, or tool output, or something so simple as a date read in a user's terminal.

Luigi Vincenzo Mancini, a professor at Sapienza University of Rome and one of the co-authors of the MaleficNet paper, advises organizations to take a defense-in-depth approach to open-weight AI security, "rather than trying to find a single magical 'AI malware scanner.'".

Like any third-party software, owners should download AI models from official sources. As an added measure, users can compare the models they download with a known, trusted baseline.

Industry observers note that "Microsoft says that reliable detection of these kinds of modifications requires being able to diff the deployed weights against the original, unmodified weights," Mancini notes. "That's a powerful argument for treating model weights more like source code or binaries than like ordinary data files.".

In a recent development, next, owners should scan their models in general for anomalies. Though as Hitaj points out, "No scan proves a model is clean, and ordinary testing rarely finds a trigger the attacker chose. So the key controls limit what a compromised model can do: give AI agents only the access they need, keep credentials and production systems out of reach, restrict network access, log what agents do, and require human approval for consequential actions. If a model turns malicious, you want it boxed in and visible.".

Beyond restricting them from the outset, "Organizations should monitor for unexpected agent behaviour at the system boundary," Mancini claims. Practically speaking, "a model emitting an unusual shell command, attempting an unexpected network connection, accessing credentials it normally doesn't need, or suddenly invoking a tool in an unusual context can be a much more actionable detection technique than directly inferring malicious intent from billions of model parameters.".

Sources indicate that he began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

Sources indicate that he holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
