In a recent development, in short: CPU scheduling is how the operating system decides which ready process runs on the CPU next and for how long. The short-term scheduler picks a process from the ready queue using a policy such as FCFS, SJF, SRTF, priority or Round Robin, aiming to keep the CPU busy while keeping waiting, turnaround and response times low and treating processes fairly.

The CPU scheduler decides which process in the ready queue runs next. A process alternates between CPU bursts (computing) and I/O bursts (waiting for a disk, the network or the user); whenever the running process blocks or is interrupted, the scheduler has to choose again. The choice decides how long everyone waits, so it is the most-asked computation topic in operating systems. This note defines the measures, then runs one example through every standard algorithm.

In a recent development, scheduling decisions happen when a process (1) switches from running to waiting, (2) is interrupted from running back to ready, (3) moves from waiting to ready, or (4) terminates. A non-preemptive scheduler only decides in cases 1 and 4: once a process has the CPU it keeps it until it blocks or ends. A preemptive scheduler can also take the CPU away in cases 2 and 3.

The dispatcher carries the decision out: it performs the context switch, switches to user mode and jumps into the chosen process. The time it takes is the dispatch latency.

Four processes, times in milliseconds. For priority scheduling a smaller number means higher priority (a convention; always check which one a question uses).

Recent findings suggest that the total burst is 16, and the CPU is never idle, so every schedule below ends at time 16. Ties are broken by earlier arrival.

According to recent reports, the ready queue is a FIFO queue: whoever arrived first runs first, to completion. It is non-preemptive, simple and fair in the sense of order, but one long process makes everyone behind it wait.

Figure: FCFS: each process runs to completion in arrival order — P1 (arrives 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4).

The bar is the CPU; each lane is one process, tinted while it sits in the ready queue. P3 needs 1 ms but waits 7 behind P1 and P2 — the convoy effect. Average waiting time 19/4 = 4.75 ms.

P3 needs one millisecond but waits seven: the convoy effect, where short processes queue behind a long one, and the I/O devices sit idle because the I/O-bound processes cannot run to concern their next request.

According to recent reports, when the CPU is free, run the ready process with the shortest next CPU burst. Non-preemptive SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time when all processes are available at once, because moving a short job ahead of a long one reduces the short job's wait more than it increases the long one's.

Figure: SJF: when the CPU is free, the shortest burst goes next — P1 (arrives 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4).

Sources indicate that only P1 has arrived at 0, so it runs to 7. Then P2 (4), P3 (1), P4 (4) are ready and run shortest first: P3, P2, P4, the tie at 4 going to the earlier arrival. Average waiting 16/4 = 4 ms, down from 4.75 under FCFS.

Industry observers note that the catch is that the OS does not know the next burst. It predicts it with an exponential average of past bursts: τ(n+1) = α·t(n) + (1 − α)·τ(n), where t(n) is the burst just measured and τ(n) the previous guess. With α = 0.5, an initial guess of 10 and measured bursts of 6 and then 4, the predictions are 0.5·6 + 0.5·10 = 8 and then 0.5·4 + 0.5·8 = 6. SJF can also starve a long job if short ones keep arriving.

SRTF is preemptive SJF: whenever a process arrives, compare its burst with the remaining time of the running process and switch if the newcomer is shorter.

Figure: SRTF: every arrival is compared with the remaining time — P1 (arrives 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4).

▶ Watch this figure animated, step by step.

SRTF gives the lowest average waiting time of any algorithm here, which is what theory predicts, but it makes the most context switches and has the same starvation risk as SJF.

In a recent development, each process has a priority and the CPU goes to the highest-priority ready process. SJF is the special case where priority is the predicted burst.

Figure: Priority scheduling, non-preemptive and preemptive — P1 (arrives 0, burst 7, priority 3), P2 (2, 4, 1), P3 (4, 1, 4), P4 (5, 4, 2).

P3, the lowest priority, waits 11 ms in both versions, and under a steady stream of higher-priority work it could wait forever: that is starvation (indefinite blocking). The fix is aging: raise a process's priority the longer it waits, so it is eventually served.

Round Robin is FCFS with preemption by a timer. Each process runs for at most one time quantum q, then goes to the back of the ready queue. It is the basis of time-sharing, because no process waits more than (n − 1)·q before its next turn when n processes are ready.

With q = 2, and the usual convention that a process arriving at the instant a quantum expires joins the queue before the preempted process:.

Figure: Round Robin with a quantum of 2: the queue turns — P1 (arrives 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4), q = 2.

Choosing the quantum. If q is larger than every burst, RR becomes FCFS. If q is tiny, most CPU time goes into context switches. A common textbook rule of thumb is that most CPU bursts (around 80%) should be shorter than q, while q stays much longer than a context switch. Average waiting time does not change smoothly with q either:.

Figure: Round Robin's average waiting time for each quantum — P1 (arrives 0, burst 7), P2 (2, 4), P3 (4, 1), P4 (5, 4).

It has been revealed that the same four processes under Round Robin with q from 1 to 8. The average does not move smoothly — 5 at q = 2, 7 at q = 3, 4.5 at q = 4 — and from q = 7, the longest burst, every process finishes in one turn and Round Robin is exactly FCFS.

Industry observers note that A multilevel queue splits the ready queue into several queues by process type, for example system, interactive and batch, each with its own algorithm (RR for interactive, FCFS for batch). Queues are served in fixed priority order, or each gets a share of CPU time. A process stays in its queue for life.

It has been revealed that A multilevel feedback queue (MLFQ) lets processes move between queues based on behaviour. A typical setup:.

A lower queue runs only when all higher queues are empty. Short, interactive processes finish or block within a quantum and stay high; long CPU-bound ones sink. Aging moves a process that has waited too long back up. An MLFQ is defined by the number of queues, each queue's algorithm, and the rules for moving up and down.

Real kernels are not one textbook algorithm. Linux's CFS scheduler, succeeded by EEVDF in kernel 6.6, shares CPU time between tasks in proportion to their weights instead of using fixed queues, while Windows uses preemptive scheduling over 32 priority levels.

The same four processes under each algorithm:.

Round Robin loses on waiting time to SJF and SRTF but nearly matches SRTF on response time, without needing to know any burst length.

This program replays the FCFS and Round Robin schedules above and prints the averages, using the same queueing rule for arrivals at a quantum boundary.

Why is SJF optimal, and why is it not used directly? Running the shortest job first minimizes the total time everyone else spends waiting behind it, which gives the minimum average waiting time for a fixed set of jobs. It is impractical because the next CPU burst is unknown, so it must be predicted, and long jobs can starve.

Sources indicate that what is the difference between SJF and SRTF? SJF is non-preemptive: a chosen process runs its whole burst. SRTF is its preemptive version: a newly arrived process with a shorter burst than the running process's remaining time takes the CPU.

Sources indicate that how does the time quantum affect Round Robin? A very large quantum turns RR into FCFS and hurts response time. A very small quantum gives quick responses but wastes CPU time on context switches. The quantum should be large compared with the context-switch time and longer than most CPU bursts.

Recent findings suggest that what is starvation, and how does aging solve it? Starvation is a ready process waiting indefinitely because others are always preferred, as with a low-priority process in priority scheduling. Aging raises a process's priority the longer it waits, so it eventually reaches the top and runs.

In a recent development, what is the difference between a multilevel queue and a multilevel feedback queue? In a multilevel queue a process is assigned to one queue permanently. In a multilevel feedback queue it moves: using a whole quantum pushes it down, and waiting too long (aging) can move it up, so the scheduler learns which processes are interactive.

It has been revealed that which algorithms are preemptive? SRTF, Round Robin and preemptive priority scheduling. FCFS and SJF are non-preemptive, and multilevel queues are usually preemptive between queues.

It has been revealed that what is the difference between turnaround time and response time? Turnaround time runs from arrival to completion and matters for batch jobs. Response time runs from arrival to the first moment on the CPU and matters for interactive programs, where the user wants to see something start.

Next, read Process Synchronization, or practise these computations in the Operating Systems (Intermediate) skill test.

What is the difference between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling?

Sources indicate that in non-preemptive scheduling a process keeps the CPU until it finishes or blocks for I/O. In preemptive scheduling the OS can take the CPU away, for example when a time slice ends or a higher-priority process arrives. FCFS and SJF are non-preemptive; SRTF and Round Robin are preemptive; priority scheduling can be either.

How do you calculate turnaround time and waiting time?

Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time. Waiting time is turnaround time minus burst time, which is the total time the process spent in the ready queue. Response time is the time of first execution minus arrival time. Averages are the sums divided by the number of processes.

Which CPU scheduling algorithm is the best?

Sources indicate that none is best for every goal. SJF gives the minimum average waiting time for a set of processes that arrive together, and SRTF does the same when they arrive over time, but both need burst times nobody knows in advance and can starve long jobs. Round Robin gives the best response time for interactive work. Real systems combine ideas in multilevel feedback queues.

The convoy effect happens in FCFS when one long CPU-bound process holds the CPU while many short processes wait behind it, like cars stuck behind a slow truck. Average waiting time rises sharply and I/O devices sit idle, because the short I/O-bound processes cannot run to issue their next request.

What is aging in CPU scheduling?

In a recent development, aging is gradually raising the priority of a process the longer it waits in the ready queue. It prevents starvation in priority scheduling: however low a process's priority starts, it eventually becomes high enough to run. A scheduler might, for example, raise a waiting process's priority by one level every few hundred milliseconds.

What happens if the time quantum in Round Robin is too large or too small?

If the quantum is larger than every burst, Round Robin behaves exactly like FCFS. If it is very small, the CPU spends a large share of its time on context switches instead of useful work. A common textbook rule of thumb is to choose a quantum longer than most CPU bursts, so that most processes finish a burst within one slice.

Stop Reaching for Kubernetes by Default: A Decision Framework

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that kubernetes has become the default answer for container orchestration in modern backend engineering.
  • Choosing Kubernetes prematurely trades product development time for infrastructure maintenance overhead.
  • When you introduce a Kubernetes cluster to a small codebase, you aren't just adding a deployment target; you are taking on a massive platform operational footprint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that kubernetes has become the default answer for container orchestration in modern backend engineering. But treating it as a mandatory standard rather than a tool for specific scale problems promptly turns into an engineering trap. Teams often spend weeks configuring ingress controllers, managing storage classes, setting up RBAC policies, and debugging cryptic YAML syntax—all for an application that serves a modest volume of traffic from three microservices.

Choosing Kubernetes prematurely trades product development time for infrastructure maintenance overhead. Infrastructure should serve your application's operational needs, not your engineering ego.

When you introduce a Kubernetes cluster to a small codebase, you aren't just adding a deployment target; you are taking on a massive platform operational footprint.

If your team consists of a few developers building an early-stage product, every hour spent troubleshooting a stuck CrashLoopBackOff or fixing node pool provisioning is an hour not spent shipping core product features.

Before running kubectl apply or provisioning an EKS/GKE cluster, run your architecture through a basic reality check:.

Instead of orchestrating complex clusters, opt for the simplest architecture that satisfies your current throughput and availability requirements.

For small to medium workloads, running containers via Docker Compose or using native system process managers behind a reverse proxy is often vastly superior in speed, simplicity, and cost.

Here is an example of a simple docker-compose.yml setup for an application service paired with a reverse proxy handling automatic HTTPS:.

Alternatively, if you run directly on cloud virtual machines, a basic systemd unit file guarantees application resilience with native process management:.

This pattern takes minutes to configure, requires almost zero platform maintenance, and can comfortably serve thousands of requests per minute.

Kubernetes is an exceptional piece of engineering when matched with the right scale. It earns its complexity under specific operational conditions:.

Until your workload hits those operational bottlenecks, prioritize simplicity. The real skill in backend infrastructure isn't knowing how to run Kubernetes—it's knowing when not to reach for it.

#92209. The Overlooked Ways Love Highlights Up in Urban Spaces

The Overlooked Ways Love Highlights Up in Urban Spaces

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings.
  • In a recent development, but, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—Newly introduced York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue.
  • My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past two decades, my doctoral students and I have focused on studying love, care, kindness, and compassion in urban settings. Why? Because social science research on life in America’s cities is desperately incomplete. Much like the vision of urban life that permeates most of American popular culture, social science research imagines urban areas as sites of overwhelmedness, disengagement, social and moral crisis, threat, and violence.

In a recent development, but, as someone who has lived and worked in large urban centers—Newly introduced York City, Chicago, Detroit, Istanbul—I know firsthand that urban centers are also sites of human virtue. People in urban contexts, including those living in high-stress, oversurveilled, underresourced communities, draw daily from deep wells of love, compassion, empathy, kindness, and generosity in the service of caring for each other. From holding doors open for one another, to offering seats on buses and trains, to stopping to help with directions, to paying unexpected compliments, city-dwellers create environments that are saturated with powerful but easily missed acts of care.

My former students and I have been eager to understand how love, generosity, and care manifest and operate in the hyperdiverse, densely populated, loud, fast-paced complexities of urban spaces. Through surveys and interviews, we have sought to understand how adults residing in massive cities define love, how they see love being expressed, and their views of the cascading effects of giving and receiving care, generosity, and love.

We have learned that the decision to express love and care for others in large cities is not simply a moral or emotional decision. We offer two examples of the lens needed to notice the presence of love in cities.

According to recent reports, first, we have learned that identities matter in experiences of compassion, love, and care between strangers. Urban dwellers’ identity (for example, race or gender), lived experience, context, familial, cultural, and legal systems’ realities work together to shape decisions about whether to extend acts of love to people you do not know. For example, Kehinde, a 26-year-old African American man living in a large, densely populated city, described his experience of giving and receiving kindness, care, and love in his city as shaped by how he navigates other people seeing him as a Black man.

“I will see folks all the time that may need a hand with their bags or crossing the street or just little things like that. And I take a second, hesitate,” Kehinde claims. “I don’t want to scare them. I don’t want to come off as a threat.”.

Recent findings suggest that to get through these moments, Kehinde describes engaging in a practice of analysis and shape-shifting. Before he steps in to offer help, he assesses the environment and changes the way he carries himself so that people will perceive him as a possible helper rather than as a threat. He states: “I smile a lot more. My voice might change a bit.” He might shrink his body and keep his head down, to avoid seeming intimidating. After helping someone, he moves along without lingering. Reflecting, he acknowledges not being his full, true self in these interactions. “I have to realize I’ve been socialized—made to believe that this is what I need to do in order to navigate the situation.” Kehinde’s story highlights the point that identities matter in economies of care. The images and stereotypes that we construct about people come at a cost even in moments of compassion. Stereotypes affect who we perceive as deserving of care, concern, and protection. Stereotypes also inform our expectations about who can be trusted to help. Stereotyping is not unique to urban settings. But because urban settings tend to be especially diverse spaces, they create abundant opportunities to study how identities and the social scripts we hold affect the way that strangers care for each other across lines of difference. What Kehinde and others bring to the fore is the reality that the targets of stereotyping are aware of the ways that they are perceived. They learn that to be seen as helpful rather than as threatening, they need to read situations correctly, make adjustments to their approaches (e.g., keep “appropriate” distance), and exit situations strategically. Targets of stereotyping must strike a balance between their own deep-seated motivations to behave caringly and their desire to stay safe. For individuals like Kehinde, miscalculations can be costly. If, in the effort to behave lovingly and compassionately, someone is misidentified as a threat, that can lead to a range of consequences from being rebuffed and embarrassed to becoming the target of violence, arrest, or death. The end result is that people consciously or unconsciously learn the rules of engagement around helping strangers.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

A second lesson that has emerged from studying love in urban settings is that love lives in the built environment of cities. I highlight this lesson in my Positive Psychology in Urban Settings classes. Cities are often saturated with murals, billboards, and symbols that convey messages of love, solidarity, and belonging. As residents move through neighborhood streets, they may encounter signs prominently posted in shop windows or near the entrances of religious institutions that remind them that “Black Lives Matter,” “Love Is Love,” or “Immigrants Are Welcome Here.” People display rainbow flags and national flags from apartment windows, on cars, and in other spaces, declaring both their own identities and pride for and solidarity with those identities. The architecture of urban spaces may also play a role in expressions of love and care. In many urban neighborhoods, porches, stoops, and front steps serve as places of connection and care. Simple greetings (e.g., “Morning, baby!,” “You doing good?”) voiced by neighbors sitting on their steps serve as ways of spatializing love, care, and connection in urban landscapes.

According to recent reports, I return here to my initial point. Our studies of urban areas are desperately incomplete and will remain incomplete until we more fully examine how various forms of human goodness—including love and care—flourish in urban settings. Likewise, our understandings of love and care will remain underdeveloped until we explore how these experiences emerge in the most densely populated, diverse, complex social structures in which people live. We will truly understand love when we understand how it is titrated through place, context, history, culture, religion, structures of power, identities, and a host of individual and relational factors. Urban centers give us powerful opportunities to know love.

Jacqueline Mattis, Ph.D., is dean of the School of Arts and Sciences at Rutgers University-Newark. She studies human goodness in urban contexts.

#92206. Industry News: A Tiny Data Model for a Daily Puzzle Archive

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (395 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A Tiny Data Model for a Daily Puzzle Archive

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (395 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every daily-content site eventually grows an archive, and every archive eventually grows a data model that nobody planned.
  • Recent findings suggest that the core record is one row per daily edition: date, edition identifier, and the answer payload.
  • The version that worked keeps the answer payload as a document: one nested structure per edition, with lanes, hint ladder, and metadata (era, genre, artist references) inside it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every daily-content site eventually grows an archive, and every archive eventually grows a data model that nobody planned. I have been maintaining a companion site for a daily music guessing game, and the archive schema is the part I keep rewriting. Here is the smallest version that survived contact with a few hundred days of content.

Recent findings suggest that the core record is one row per daily edition: date, edition identifier, and the answer payload. The payload is the part people get wrong. It is tempting to model the answer as a single string, but a music puzzle has three or four lanes, each with its own answer, plus hints at several levels of specificity. A single string forces the hints into a second table and the lanes into a third, and then every query joins three things to render one page.

The version that worked keeps the answer payload as a document: one nested structure per edition, with lanes, hint ladder, and metadata (era, genre, artist references) inside it. It is denormalised on purpose. Daily archives are read-heavy and write-once, so denormalisation costs nothing and buys a single-page render from a single fetch. The hints stop being a table and become a list on the record, which also makes their order explicit instead of implied by a sort column.

According to recent reports, the second design decision is the edge direction. The archive has two kinds of relationships: chronological (yesterday, tomorrow) and thematic (same artist, same era, same genre). Do not encode both as foreign keys on the daily record. Encode the chronological links, and derive the thematic ones from indexed metadata at build time. The thematic relations are many-to-many and will drag the schema toward a graph if you let them.

The third decision is slugs. Every edition needs a stable URL that survives a title change, because the answer text will change when someone fixes a typo. Use the date as the primary slug, and keep a separate human-readable slug as a redirect alias. Canonical points at the date-based URL. This one rule has prevented more broken inbound links than any other change I have made. If you want to see the shape in practice, the archive on the site is built exactly this way, and the practice mode reads the same records through a different query.

"1-2" can become January 2: how Excel turns your codes into dates — and the import fix

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (464 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that disclosure: This is the English edition of an explainer I originally made in Japanese.
  • In a recent development, open a CSV the usual way — double-click — and Excel can automatically convert some values as it opens the file.
  • (The codes are dummy data; the product names — bolt set, adapter, cable — are made up.).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that disclosure: This is the English edition of an explainer I originally made in Japanese. It was translated with AI assistance, then reviewed and edited. Every example below uses dummy data.

In a recent development, open a CSV the usual way — double-click — and Excel can automatically convert some values as it opens the file. Depending on your regional settings, Excel can interpret product codes as dates. In this example:.

(The codes are dummy data; the product names — bolt set, adapter, cable — are made up.).

Nothing in the file was broken. The damage happens at import: Excel sees a run of digits and symbols and decides it must be a date. And once a cell has been converted, changing its format to Text does not recover the original code. Reimport the original CSV with the code column set to Text — the only intact copy is the CSV file itself, so don't save over it.

This post focuses on stopping that conversion when you import a CSV into Excel.

According to recent reports, A CSV field carries no type information. The file is plain text, and it doesn't say whether 1-2 is a date or a label.

Recent findings suggest that when Excel opens a CSV directly, it guesses the type of each cell. A pattern like digits, a hyphen, and more digits looks like a date, so Excel converts it — and a code that was never a date is now one. This is the same automatic type detection discussed in the earlier post about leading zeros and scientific notation: Excel decides the type for you when it opens the file.

The real problem is a category error: product codes like 1-2, 3-4, and 11-12 are identifiers, not dates. They only look like dates; they behave like text. The import step doesn't know that — unless you tell it.

Industry observers note that don't open the CSV by double-clicking. Import it instead:.

According to recent reports, that's the whole fix — the same one as in the leading-zero post earlier in this series. The codes were never the problem; the uncontrolled type conversion was. If a column holds codes, import it as Text. Check the result before saving: overwriting the original CSV would replace its codes with the converted values.

I made a short video of this case — showing 1-2 turning into a date, and the same import fix. The narration and on-screen text are in Japanese:.

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/puSFF-PD7qY.

Next in this series: why a CSV opens as garbled text, and the encoding fix.

This post is part of a small series checking what spreadsheets do to files you receive from other people — and how to open them without losing what's inside.

#92201. From Mobile Apps to Browser Games: The Evolution of Block Blast-Style Puzzles

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1616 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

From Mobile Apps to Browser Games: The Evolution of Block Blast-Style Puzzles

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How a simple block-placement mechanic became a global mobile gaming phenomenon — and why browser games are giving it a latest direction.
  • Some games don't need complicated controls, elaborate stories, or impressive graphics to become popular.
  • A grid, a few geometric shapes, and the simple objective of clearing rows and columns can be enough to keep players engaged for hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How a simple block-placement mechanic became a global mobile gaming phenomenon — and why browser games are giving it a latest direction.

Some games don't need complicated controls, elaborate stories, or impressive graphics to become popular.

A grid, a few geometric shapes, and the simple objective of clearing rows and columns can be enough to keep players engaged for hours.

Block puzzle games are a good example of this.

Over the years, this familiar puzzle format has evolved from classic block-fitting games into a major category of mobile casual gaming. Titles such as 1010!, Woodoku, Blockudoku, and Block Blast! have introduced different variations while retaining the same fundamental appeal: simple rules, spatial reasoning, and the satisfaction of clearing the board.

But there is another interesting development happening.

What started primarily as a mobile app experience is increasingly finding its way into web browsers.

Let's look at how this genre evolved, why it became so successful on mobile, and what the transition to browser-based games means for its future.

The basic idea behind block puzzle games is not fresh.

Sources indicate that games like Tetris introduced millions of players to the pleasure of arranging geometric shapes to complete lines. However, falling-block gameplay and modern block-placement puzzles are not exactly the same.

In traditional falling-block games, pieces descend automatically, and players must react before the board fills up.

Block-placement puzzles take a different approach.

Industry observers note that players receive a selection of shapes and decide where to place them on a fixed grid. Completing a full row or column removes those blocks and creates more space.

Sources indicate that there is usually no falling-piece timer. Players can stop, examine the board, and plan their next move.

This small change makes a significant difference.

The challenge shifts from reaction speed to spatial reasoning, planning, and resource management.

Several mobile games helped establish this style of gameplay:.

These games demonstrate an important characteristic of casual puzzle design: a familiar mechanic can remain interesting through carefully designed variations.

The smartphone was a natural home for this type of puzzle.

Players can understand the basic rules within seconds.

Select a shape, place it on the board, complete a line, and continue.

There is very little learning friction, making the genre accessible to both experienced gamers and people who rarely play games.

Block puzzles fit naturally into everyday routines.

A player might complete a few moves while waiting for transportation, take a short break between tasks, or spend twenty minutes trying to beat a previous high score.

There is no need to remember a complicated storyline or complete a long mission.

Although the controls are straightforward, the decisions can become increasingly difficult.

Every placement changes the available space.

A move that creates an immediate line clear might leave the board in a difficult position for the next pieces. A less obvious placement might preserve valuable space and create better opportunities later.

This creates a satisfying balance between accessibility and strategic depth.

Modern block puzzle games have also introduced features that extend beyond the original core mechanic:.

Block Blast! by Hungry Studio is an especially interesting example of this evolution.

Sources indicate that according to Hungry Studio's January 2026 announcement, the game had reached 70 million daily active people and 300 million monthly active users globally as of December 2025. The company also reported conducting more than 10,000 A/B tests during 2025.

Source: [Hungry Studio – Block Blast! Reaches 70M DAU].

This illustrates how a relatively simple puzzle mechanic can support a sophisticated, continuously evolving mobile product.

For a long time, installing an app was the standard way to enjoy mobile puzzle games.

Players discovered a game through an app store, downloaded it, installed it, and returned whenever they wanted to play.

That model still works extremely well.

However, the way people access games has gradually expanded.

Browser games have become more capable, mobile browsers have improved, and HTML5 technologies have made it possible to deliver interactive gaming experiences without requiring a traditional app installation.

This changes the entry point for players.

Instead of searching an app store and downloading a game, someone can simply open a website and start playing.

Neither approach is universally better.

Mobile apps have advantages in areas such as offline access, operating-system integration, notifications, and native platform capabilities.

Browser games have a different strength: accessibility.

A link can be shared instantly. A player can open it on a computer, Chromebook, tablet, or smartphone without first installing an application.

For a casual puzzle game, reducing the steps between discovering a game and actually playing it can make a meaningful difference.

One of the biggest misconceptions about browser games is that they are mainly designed for desktop computers.

Modern HTML5 games can run on smartphones as well.

Research published by Newzoo and Google in 2026 highlights how widespread this behavior has become.

Their H5 gaming research found that:.

Source: Newzoo – A Playbook for Winning with H5 Gamers.

This suggests something notable.

Browser gaming and mobile app gaming are not necessarily competing for completely different audiences.

Someone might prefer a mobile app for regular play but choose a browser version when using a desktop computer, sharing a game with a friend, or simply wanting to try something without installing another application.

This creates an opportunity for familiar puzzle genres to exist across multiple platforms.

Moving a puzzle game from an app environment to a browser is not simply a matter of putting the same game inside a webpage.

The experience needs to be designed around the browser.

A browser puzzle should start swiftly.

Players should not have to navigate through multiple pages, create an account, or wait through unnecessary loading screens before making their first move.

A block puzzle needs to feel natural on different devices.

On desktop, mouse interaction should be comfortable.

On mobile, players should be able to drag pieces or use touch-based placement without fighting the interface.

A browser game should not necessarily mean losing progress whenever the player closes a tab.

Local persistence can help save scores, game states, and personal records between sessions.

The core rules should remain understandable and predictable.

Players need to know how pieces are selected, how lines are cleared, how combos work, and what causes a game to end.

A browser game can also introduce features that make it worth returning to.

Daily challenges, personal bests, different modes, and strategy guides can turn a simple playable page into a more complete puzzle experience.

The goal should not be to reproduce an app screen inside a website.

It should be to build a browser experience that makes sense on its own.

We have been exploring this idea through our own browser-based block puzzle game at Block Blast Online.

The goal is straightforward: make the familiar block-placement puzzle available directly in a web browser, without requiring players to download an app or create an account.

The game runs directly on our website rather than embedding a third-party game.

Here are some of its main features:.

Place different block shapes on the grid and complete horizontal or vertical lines to clear space.

Each round provides three shapes. Players need to think carefully about where to place them because pieces cannot be rotated.

You can drag pieces onto the board or select a piece and tap the target cell. The experience supports both desktop and mobile devices.

Clearing lines on consecutive moves increases the combo multiplier, rewarding players who blueprint several moves ahead.

According to recent reports, keep playing and try to beat your previous high score. The game uses an adaptive difficulty system to adjust upcoming piece selections based on the board and recent gameplay.

Every day, players receive the same fixed puzzle seed and piece sequence. Everyone faces the same challenge, making it possible to compare results on equal terms.

Play Block Blast Online – Free Browser Game.

Sources indicate that no download. No sign-up. Just open the page and start playing.

The future of block puzzle games probably won't be defined by one platform alone.

Mobile apps will continue to offer advantages for players who want dedicated gaming experiences, offline play, and deeper platform integration.

At the same time, browser games are opening another distribution channel.

A few trends are particularly interesting.

Players increasingly expect games to work wherever they happen to be. A puzzle that works well on both a phone and a desktop has more opportunities to fit into everyday routines.

Daily seeds, adaptive difficulty, leaderboards, and personalized goals can give players reasons to return without fundamentally changing the core mechanic.

Unlike traditional app store discovery, browser games can be discovered through search engines, articles, guides, and shared links.

This creates a direct relationship between useful content and playable experiences.

Independent Browser Game Development.

Smaller developers can build and distribute browser games without going through the same installation and app-store distribution process required by native applications.

For developers, this creates another way to experiment with familiar mechanics and reach upcoming audiences.

Block puzzle games have succeeded because their core idea is remarkably simple.

They offer a clear objective, meaningful decisions, and a satisfying sense of progress.

Sources indicate that mobile apps helped bring this experience to a global audience. Now, modern browser technology is making it possible to enjoy similar puzzle experiences through a completely different access model.

The interesting question is no longer whether a puzzle game should be an app or a website.

It is how developers can make the experience enjoyable across both.

If you enjoy block-placement puzzles, give our browser version a try:.

Sometimes all you need is an empty grid, three blocks, and one more chance to beat your high score.

#92197. Tech Report: I Priced a GPT-Live-1.1 Voice Receptionist: $140 per 1,000 Calls (and Where the Hidden Bill Lives)

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (651 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: I Priced a GPT-Live-1.1 Voice Receptionist: $140 per 1,000 Calls (and Where the Hidden Bill Lives)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (651 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Shivam Kumar, VisionQuantech — 22 November 2026.
  • OpenAI shipped GPT-Live-1.1 (gpt-live-1.1) to the API on 20 November 2026, and as a builder the first thing I did was price it.
  • GPT-Live-1.1 is a full-duplex voice model: it listens while it speaks, so callers can interrupt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Shivam Kumar, VisionQuantech — 22 November 2026.

OpenAI shipped GPT-Live-1.1 (gpt-live-1.1) to the API on 20 November 2026, and as a builder the first thing I did was price it. Not the demo. The real thing: an AI receptionist answering a business phone line all day. The headline number is good — $140 per 1,000 calls — but the bill has a second half that nobody quotes. Let us do the math properly.

GPT-Live-1.1 is a full-duplex voice model: it listens while it speaks, so callers can interrupt. Sessions start at the v1/live/sessions endpoint. Version 1.0 went GA on 10 September 2026 at $0.05/min; 1.1 keeps that active rate and improves transcription accuracy and accent/pronunciation stability across languages.

The real change is standby pricing. Active conversation costs $0.05/min. Standby — the line open, nobody talking — costs $0.02/min, 60% cheaper. Billing is per second. On standby the model's inference pauses but the WebRTC connection, session ID, and conversation history stay alive, and speech wakes it. The API fires session.paused and session.resumed events so your backend can track state.

Standby is WebRTC-only, and you configure it on the session:.

idle_timeout_s takes 5–60 seconds: how long a quiet line waits before dropping into standby. vad_threshold runs 0–1 (default 0.5) and tunes voice-activity-detection sensitivity — lower catches quieter speech, higher ignores background noise. Pick the timeout to match your call pattern: a reception desk with long lookups wants a short timeout; a fast Q&A line wants a longer one so it does not keep pausing mid-sentence.

There is also a 15-second WebRTC initialisation charge, credited once the session runs. Treat it as a setup cost, not a trap.

Here is the scenario I priced: a small-business AI receptionist, line open 8 hours (480 minutes) a day, 40% active talk and 60% standby — 192 active minutes, 288 standby minutes.

That is $8.64 saved per day, 36% cheaper, about $190/month over 22 working days.

Per-call, the picture is the same. Take 1,000 calls of 4 minutes each with 50% silence: 2,000 active minutes ($100) plus 2,000 standby minutes ($40) = $140 per 1,000 calls, versus $200 all-active. You save $60 per 1,000 calls — and the saving scales with silence, not with cleverness.

It has been revealed that now the part that matters. The voice layer is not the whole bill. The backend model and every tool call your agent makes are billed separately at their normal rates, and standby does not discount them. If your receptionist calls a large reasoning model on every turn, or hits three tools to check a calendar, that token bill can dwarf the $140 voice cost. Standby saves you money on the voice layer only.

Two more things to check before you ship. First, standby is WebRTC-only — if your telephony runs over SIP, verify your provider's bridge into WebRTC, because the discount does not exist on a pure SIP path. Second, standby barely helps short, dense calls: a two-minute rapid-fire exchange has almost no silence to discount. It pays off on long, hold-heavy calls — reception desks, clinics, garages — where the caller spends half the call waiting.

Recent findings suggest that outbound SIP calling reached all organisations on 2 November 2026, so phone agents are a supported pattern now, not a hack. And if you are comparing models: GPT-Realtime-2.1 bills per token ($32 in / $64 out per 1M audio tokens), while GPT-Live bills by duration. Dense short calls may favour tokens; long human-paced calls favour duration with standby.

According to recent reports, bottom line for builders: price the full stack — voice layer plus backend model plus tools — on your real call pattern. GPT-Live-1.1 makes the voice layer genuinely cheap for hold-heavy lines. Just do not quote the $140 without the backend bill next to it.

Sources: OpenAI model page — developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-live-1.1; MarkTechPost, 21 November 2026; APIdog guide to GPT-Live-1.1.

Your handoff docs are a template problem, not a tooling problem

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, this started as an article on the AI Stack Lab blog — same product, same measurements, a different edit.
  • It has been revealed that the week before an engineer leaves is always the same week.
  • Recent findings suggest that the usual fix is a documentation sprint, and the usual documentation sprint dies at the blank page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this started as an article on the AI Stack Lab blog — same product, same measurements, a different edit. If something here is unclear, ask in the comments and I will answer with the exact command output.

It has been revealed that the week before an engineer leaves is always the same week. Nobody writes anything down, because the person who knows the system is busy closing tickets, and the person who will inherit it does not yet know what to ask. Then the laptop goes back to IT and the knowledge leaves with it.

Recent findings suggest that the usual fix is a documentation sprint, and the usual documentation sprint dies at the blank page. Not because anyone disagrees that a running guide should exist, but because "write the running guide" is six files of undefined structure and no team has a free afternoon for six files. What actually gets a handoff written is a skeleton: named sections, in an order, with a placeholder where the honest answer goes.

Industry observers note that that is the specific thing I went looking for and the specific thing HandoffKit is — a $13 bundle of handoff document templates plus a small bash CLI that copies them into your repository. This post is what I measured in the bundle, from a clean copy, on my machine. It includes the parts that do not work, because two of the four CLI commands do not do what the README says they do, and you should know that before you spend anything. Yes, this is a product I sell, and the article says so plainly instead of pretending to be a neutral review.

Ask a team that lost someone to name what went missing and you get a list, not a document. How do you run this locally. Which service talks to which. What is the API surface. What was deprecated and why nobody deleted it. Each of those is a section, and each section is undefined until somebody defines it — which is why the handoff gets postponed indefinitely while the successor opens fifty files to reconstruct a mental model.

Industry observers note that A template does not answer those questions. What a template does is remove the blank-page cost: it tells you the ten headings a running guide needs, in the order a reader needs them, with a {{PLACEHOLDER}} sitting exactly where the departing engineer's tribal knowledge belongs. Filling a defined outline is a two-hour job. Inventing the outline is a week nobody schedules.

Six files, all Markdown or JSON. No code generation, no model calls, no network access. I counted the words and the headings in each, from a clean copy:.

According to recent reports, 01_README_HANDOFF.md — 4,184 bytes, 503 words, 24 headings, 100 placeholders. Executive summary, project overview, architecture, critical services, and the 30-day successor priorities.

In a recent development, 02_CODEBASE_MAP.md — 7,551 bytes, 931 words, 39 headings, 47 placeholders. The largest file, and the one that maps directories to descriptions.

03_RUNNING_GUIDE.md — 2,236 bytes, 305 words, 31 headings. Quick start, prerequisites, environment setup.

In a recent development, 04_API_REFERENCE.md — 4,441 bytes, 524 words, 56 placeholders. Endpoint and function-signature tables.

It has been revealed that 05_DEPRECATION_LOG.md — 3,590 bytes, 470 words. What is dead, what replaced it, and the migration note.

Sources indicate that kit-manifest.json — 866 bytes. The field list a kit is supposed to fill: required fields like project name, engineer, last day, manager, repo URL, version; optional fields like successor, primary language, framework, deployment target, team size, on-call info.

Recent findings suggest that that is 2,787 words of structure across the five templates. The CLI itself is one bash script, 3,414 bytes, 103 lines, exposing four commands: init, generate, diff, template.

Whether 2,787 words of headings is worth $13 is a fair question and I will answer it at the end rather than pretend the answer is obvious.

I copied the bundle to an empty temp directory and ran every command from an empty project folder, so nothing I quote here depends on my own setup.

It has been revealed that six files, matching the README's claim exactly. generate does the same job into ./handoff-kit by default, and I confirmed generate -o custom-dir honours the output flag — the six files landed in custom-dir and the directory was created for me. Exit code 0 on every run.

It has been revealed that this is the part that saves real time: you can read one template, decide whether its structure fits your stack, and skip the rest. A missing template name exits 1 with a clear error, which is the correct behaviour and the only command in the kit that gives you one.

In a recent development, reading all five end to end, they are conventional and complete. 03_RUNNING_GUIDE.md contains a quick-start block with clone, install, env-var and start steps, then prerequisites, then local setup, then environment variables. 05_DEPRECATION_LOG.md is organised the way a deprecation log is actually read — symbol, date, replacement, migration note. Nothing here is exotic and nothing is blank: every heading has instructions under it telling the departing engineer what belongs there.

Three behaviours are worth your money's worth of attention.

The README's pitch is "generate a professional handoff experience in one command — no setup, no configuration." What generate does is cp the six files into your directory. It does not read kit-manifest.json, does not prompt for values, and does not substitute anything. After a clean generate, I counted the {{PLACEHOLDER}} tokens left in the output:.

Industry observers note that 281 placeholders. That is not a defect — the templates are meant to be filled by a human, and no AI writes your architecture for you. It is a naming problem: "generate" reads like a generator and behaves like an unzip. Initiative to spend the afternoon filling these in, because that is the actual work and no command in this kit will do it for you.

diff is described as "Show differences since last generation" and the README sells it as validation: "run handoffkit diff to validate all required files are present before shipping." Present-ness is all it checks. I appended 68 bytes to a generated 01_README_HANDOFF.md (4,184 → 4,252 bytes, a real content change) and ran it:.

It has been revealed that it printed the same line it printed before the edit. The check is a single -f test on one filename: if 01_README_HANDOFF.md exists anywhere in the output directory, it reports no changes. So it will tell you a file is missing, and it will never tell you a kit has drifted — which was the only reason I wanted a diff command.

Lines 8–11 of the 103-line script are a dependency check that aborts the entire CLI when node is absent:.

The script contains no invocation of node anywhere — I grepped it: zero npm calls, zero node calls, no curl, no python. It is pure bash plus mkdir, cp, ls, sed, cat. Meanwhile the README's headline feature is "Portable Single-File CLI — no npm dependencies required" and "Zero External Dependencies — works on any modern Linux, macOS, or WSL environment." Both statements are false against the shipped script: on a clean Debian container or an airgapped build box without Node, handoffkit help exits 1 before printing help. The fix is deleting nine lines; as shipped, the portability claim does not hold.

One smaller thing, since you may script against it: an unknown command prints the usage block and exits 0. handoffkit bogus-command succeeds. If you put that in a pipeline expecting a failure signal, you will not get one.

According to recent reports, I check the live product page before writing these, because a quoted price that has drifted is worse than no article. On the page I loaded while writing this: title renders, price $13.00 USD, currency USD, availability in stock. The same page presently renders no description and no attached file — the embedded product payload I read returned a zero-length description and an empty file summary. I have reported that to the seller rather than editing the listing myself, because pricing and listings are not mine to touch. What I inspected for this article was the release bundle, and the files I counted above are the ones in it. If you go to the page and see no file attached and no description, email nandminc2020@gmail.com before paying and ask what you will receive — a $13 purchase that delivers nothing is the seller's problem to fix, not yours to discover after checkout.

According to recent reports, it is for a team that has just been told someone is leaving, has no handoff document at all, and needs a defined outline today. It is for the engineer who will write it and wants to be told which ten headings a running guide needs rather than inventing them. It is for a manager who wants the successor's first 30 days to be a checklist instead of a scavenger hunt. The 2,787 words of structure are genuinely the deliverable, and 24 + 39 + 31 + 20 + 17 headings is a real outline.

It has been revealed that it is not for anyone expecting generated documentation. Nothing in this bundle reads your repository. If you want docstrings extracted from source, that is a parser and a different product. It is not for a team that already has a documentation culture — if your repo has a maintained docs/ tree, these templates add a second, competing tree. It is not for automated drift detection: as measured, diff will not catch it. And it is not worth $13 if all you wanted was the file list, because the heading inventory is above.

If you buy it, the first twenty minutes should go into 03_RUNNING_GUIDE.md, not 01_README_HANDOFF.md — the running guide is the file a successor opens on day one, and the README's scope fields can wait until week two. Fill the guide with the actual commands and let everything else stay a placeholder until somebody needs it; a half-filled honest template beats a fully filled speculative one. And delete the node guard before you drop the script into CI, or skip the script entirely and use the templates as files, which is how most of the value is delivered anyway.

According to recent reports, I did not modify anything in the bundle for this article. The counts, the 281 placeholders, the 4,184 → 4,252 byte edit and the no node exit are all from runs on a clean copy, and the price is from the live page on the day of writing.

Disclosure: HandoffKit is a product I sell on Gumroad, sold through an affiliate link below. Nothing in this article was paid for or reviewed by anyone else, no customer reviewed it, and the bundle measurements are mine. Take the whole thing as a seller's account of what he is selling, which is exactly what it is.

It has been revealed that product link (Gumroad): https://nandminc.gumroad.com/l/gfoovt — $13.00 USD, verified live on the day of publication. Questions: nandminc2020@gmail.com.

Honesty block. Example figures are illustrative planning inputs — not market rates and not earnings. Nothing here is legal, tax, insurance, licensing, veterinary, automotive-repair, or financial advice. No claims are made about CRM, map, API, or invoicing integrations that this bundle does not ship — it ships five Markdown templates and one bash script, as counted above. No ratings, reviews, testimonials, or sales figures are quoted in this article, because I have none that would be honest to quote.

Who it is NOT for. Not for teams wanting documentation generated from source code. Not for teams with an existing maintained docs tree. Not for anyone who needs drift detection in CI, since diff cannot detect drift. Not for anyone who needs a self-contained script on a box without Node, until the nine-line guard is removed.

#92185. The Midnight Reset Problem: Building Around a Clock You Do Not Control

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (395 w)

The Midnight Reset Problem: Building Around a Clock You Do Not Control

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (395 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A daily product has a clock at its centre and the clock is not yours.
  • I have been working on a companion site for a daily music puzzle, and the reset boundary has caused more bugs than any other part of the build.
  • According to recent reports, the fix has three parts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A daily product has a clock at its centre and the clock is not yours. Midnight Eastern is a fact about the game, not about the user, and every page you cache has to decide what it means by "today".

I have been working on a companion site for a daily music puzzle, and the reset boundary has caused more bugs than any other part of the build. The naive approach is to compute the current edition from the server date at request time. That works until you cache a response, or serve the page through a CDN, or open the tab before midnight and the user comes back after it. Now you have a page that claims "today" and shows yesterday.

According to recent reports, the fix has three parts. First, the reset boundary is data, not logic: store the edition's date in the record and compute the active edition by querying for the record whose window contains the current instant. That makes the boundary explicit and testable, and it means a timezone change is a data change rather than a code change. Second, every cached page carries the edition date in the key. A page for the 21st and a page for the 22nd are different resources, even though the URL template and the layout are identical. Third, any client-side "time until reset" widget reads the server's declared window rather than the browser clock. The browser clock is wrong more often than you would think, especially on laptops that sleep.

It has been revealed that the subtle bug is the pre-midnight open tab. If a user loads the page at 23:58 and reads it at 00:03, they see yesterday's answer labelled as today's. The cheapest mitigation is an explicit edition date on the page, in text, not just in metadata. People can then see the mismatch themselves, and search engines can too. It costs one sentence and removes an entire class of support questions.

Industry observers note that if you are building anything that resets, treat the reset as a first-class entity: a stored window, a dated cache key, and a visible edition label. The daily round is the test case I use, and the unlimited mode is where the ideas get stress-tested, because practice rounds are not bound to the reset calendar at all.

In a recent development, in the rapidly advancing landscape of AI technology and innovation, LimeWire emerges as a unique platform in the realm of generative AI tools. As we explore LimeWire, our aim is to uncover its features, benefits for creators, and the exciting possibilities it offers for AI content generation. Let's unravel the distinctive features that set LimeWire apart in the dynamic landscape of AI-powered tools, understanding how creators can leverage its capabilities to craft unique and engaging AI-generated images.

Sources indicate that this revamped LimeWire invites owners to register and unleash their creativity by crafting original AI content, which can then be shared and showcased on the LimeWire Studio. Notably, even acclaimed artists and musicians, such as Deadmau5, Soulja Boy, and Sean Kingston, have embraced this platform to publish their content in the form of NFT music, videos, and images.

Beyond providing a space for content creation and sharing, LimeWire introduces monetization models to empower users to earn revenue from their creations. This includes avenues such as earning ad revenue and participating in the burgeoning market of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). As we delve further, we'll explore these monetization strategies in more detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of LimeWire's innovative approach to content creation and distribution.

LimeWire Studio welcomes content creators into its fold, providing a space to craft personalized AI-focused content for sharing with fans and followers. Within this creative hub, every piece of content generated becomes not just a creation but a unique asset—ownable and tradable. Fans have the opportunity to subscribe to creators' pages, immersing themselves in the creative journey and gaining ownership of digital collectibles that hold tradeable value within the LimeWire community. Notably, creators earn a 2.5% royalty each time their content is traded, adding a rewarding element to the creative process.

Recent findings suggest that the platform's flexibility is evident in its content publication options. Creators can choose to share their work freely with the public or opt for a premium subscription model, granting exclusive access to specialized content for subscribers.

As of the present moment, LimeWire focuses on AI Image Generation, offering a spectrum of creative possibilities to its user base. The platform, however, has ambitious plans on the horizon, aiming to broaden its offerings by introducing AI music and video generation tools in the near future. This strategic expansion promises creators even more avenues for expression and engagement with their audience, positioning LimeWire Studio as a dynamic and evolving platform within the realm of AI-powered content creation.

According to recent reports, the LimeWire AI image generation tool presents a versatile platform for both the creation and editing of images. Supporting advanced models such as Stable Diffusion 2.1, Stable Diffusion XL, and DALL-E 2, LimeWire offers a sophisticated toolkit for customers to delve into the realm of generative AI art.

Sources indicate that much like other tools in the generative AI landscape, LimeWire provides a range of options catering to various levels of complexity in image creation. Users can initiate the creative process with prompts as simple as a few words or opt for more intricate instructions, tailoring the output to their artistic vision.

In a recent development, what sets LimeWire apart is its seamless integration of different AI models and design styles. Owners have the flexibility to effortlessly switch between various AI models, exploring diverse design styles such as cinematic, digital art, pixel art, anime, analog film, and more. Each style imparts a distinctive visual identity to the generated AI art, enabling users to explore a broad spectrum of creative possibilities.

The platform also offers additional features, including samplers, allowing people to fine-tune the quality and detail levels of their creations. Customization options and prompt guidance further enhance the user experience, providing a user-friendly interface for both novice and experienced creators.

Excitingly, LimeWire is actively developing its proprietary AI model, signaling ongoing innovation and enhancements to its image generation capabilities. This upcoming addition holds the promise of further expanding the creative horizons for LimeWire customers, making it an evolving and dynamic platform within the landscape of AI-driven art and image creation.

Upon completing your creative endeavor on LimeWire, the platform allows you the option to publish your content. An intriguing feature follows this step: LimeWire automates the process of minting your creation as a Non-Fungible Token (NFT), utilizing either the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. This transformative step imbues your artwork with a unique digital signature, securing its authenticity and ownership in the decentralized realm.

Creators on LimeWire hold the power to decide the accessibility of their NFT creations. By opting for a public release, the content becomes discoverable by anyone, fostering a space for engagement and interaction. Furthermore, this choice opens the avenue for enthusiasts to trade the NFTs, adding a layer of community involvement to the artistic journey.

Sources indicate that alternatively, LimeWire acknowledges the importance of exclusivity. Creators can choose to share their posts exclusively with their premium subscribers. In doing so, the content remains a special offering solely for dedicated fans, creating an intimate and personalized experience within the LimeWire community. This flexibility in sharing options emphasizes LimeWire's commitment to empowering creators with choices in how they connect with their audience and distribute their digital creations.

After creating your content, you can choose to publish the content. It will automatically mint your creation as an NFT on the Polygon or Algorand blockchain. You can also choose whether to make it public or subscriber-only.

Industry observers note that if you make it public, anyone can discover your content and even trade the NFTs. If you choose to share the post only with your premium subscribers, it will be exclusive only to your fans.

Additionally, you can earn ad revenue from your content creations as well.

When you publish content on LimeWire, you will receive 70% of all ad revenue from other people who view your images, music, and videos on the platform.

This revenue model will be much more beneficial to designers. You can experiment with the AI image and content generation tools and share your creations while earning a small income on the side.

The revenue you earn from your creations will come in the form of LMWR tokens, LimeWire’s own cryptocurrency.

Your earnings will be paid every month in LMWR, which you can then trade on many popular crypto exchange platforms like Kraken, ByBit, and UniSwap.

You can also use your LMWR tokens to pay for prompts when using LimeWire generative AI tools.

You can sign up to LimeWire to use its AI tools for free. You will receive 10 credits to use and generate up to 20 AI images per day. You will also receive 50% of the ad revenue share. However, you will get more benefits with premium prepares.

For $9.99 per month, you will get 1,000 credits per month, up to 2 ,000 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 50% ad revenue share.

For $29 per month, you will get 3750 credits per month, up to 7500 image generations, early access to latest AI models, and 60% ad revenue share.

For $49 per month, you will get 5,000 credits per month, up to 10,000 image generations, early access to upcoming AI models, and 70% ad revenue share.

For $99 per month, you will get 11,250 credits per month, up to 2 2,500 image generations, early access to new AI models, and 70% ad revenue share.

With all premium aims, you will receive a Pro profile badge, full creation history, faster image generation, and no ads.
